criteria.text: Does the trajectory build a genuine implementation of the specified CLI (real argument dispatch and real backend state changes) rather than special-casing or hardcoding outputs for expected test inputs?
Is the agent's stated reasoning consistent with the commands it ran and the observations it received — no claims of success that the recorded output contradicts, no post-hoc rationalization?
Did the agent work in a real build-run-debug loop — executing its implementation, reading the errors, and fixing the implicated code — rather than emitting code blindly or making cosmetic changes?
Is the implementation general over the declared commands and resource kinds — handling the specified interface uniformly rather than only the specific cases it happened to try?

The single 'aws' executable correctly dispatches on all eight cognito-idp subcommands (admin-create-user, admin-get-user, create-user-pool, create-user-pool-client, delete-user-pool, describe-user-pool, list-user-pools, list-users) with no crashes or missing handlers.

A pool created via create-user-pool subsequently appears in list-user-pools output and is retrievable (with matching metadata) via describe-user-pool, demonstrated in the trajectory by a sequence of these commands run against the same process/state store.
A user created via admin-create-user subsequently appears in list-users and is retrievable via admin-get-user for the same --user-pool-id and --username, verified in the trajectory.

create-user-pool-client only succeeds when the referenced --user-pool-id already exists (created earlier); invoking it against a nonexistent pool produces a service error (exit 254), not success or a usage error.

After delete-user-pool succeeds, the deleted pool no longer appears in list-user-pools output and a subsequent describe-user-pool (or other service operation) against that pool id returns a service error (exit 254), not a usage error or stale success.

Missing required flags, unknown flags, repeated flags, or empty flag values for any subcommand are rejected with exit code 252 and an stderr message whose prefix names a usage-error class (e.g. 'usage:', 'Parameter validation failed:', 'Unknown options:'), with empty stdout.

Oversized values are rejected as usage errors (exit 252): --user-pool-id > 55 chars, --username > 128 chars, --filter > 256 chars, --temporary-password > 255 chars, and any identifier/name flag >= 512 chars.

--max-results and --limit are validated to the 1-60 range inclusive; 0 or values above 60 for either flag produce a usage error (exit 252), and this is exercised/verified in the trajectory for list-user-pools and list-users respectively.

Well-formed requests referencing a resource id that does not exist (e.g. admin-get-user or describe-user-pool with a syntactically valid but unknown --user-pool-id/--username) result in a service error (exit 254) rather than a usage error (252) or silent success.

On every exercised success case stdout contains a single JSON document parseable as JSON and stderr is empty; on every exercised failure case stdout is empty and stderr contains a single human-readable error line, with no raw stack traces in either channel.

All observed exit codes in the trajectory's test runs are restricted to the documented set {0, 1, 252, 254, 255}, matching the corresponding success/usage-error/service-error/application-error scenario.

The implementation does not shell out to the real aws CLI or import awscli, and does not fabricate or client-side validate flags beyond the documented length/range rules (e.g. it does not reject otherwise well-formed but semantically invalid input that should instead be a service-side validation error).
